headline: 12-year Cinebench record shattered by ancient Intel Core i5 4670K
summary: An overclocking enthusiast has set a new world record in Cinebench R11.5 using a decade-old Intel CPU, liquid nitrogen, and a modest DDR3 setup.
details: Overclocking expert Luumi has achieved a remarkable feat, breaking a 12-year-old Cinebench R11.5 world record for the Intel Core i5 4670K. The record-breaking score of 10.8 cb was achieved using the Haswell-era quad-core CPU, pushed to an astonishing 6,301 MHz with the aid of liquid nitrogen cooling.

The system featured an ASRock Z97 OC Formula motherboard and 4GB of XPG DDR3 RAM, powered by a Corsair AXi 1600 PSU. This achievement highlights that cutting-edge hardware isn't always necessary to set new performance benchmarks in the overclocking community.
This record is specific to the Core i5 4670K processor category. Despite its age, the 22nm Haswell chip, originally released with a base clock of 3.4 GHz, was pushed to its absolute limits.

The use of older hardware for such achievements is a breath of fresh air for many in the overclocking scene, with community members noting the rarity of seeing results that don't involve the latest X3D CPUs or high-end GPUs.
Luumi utilized Windows 7 64-bit Pro for the benchmark, a common practice for ensuring compatibility and stability with older hardware during extreme overclocking attempts.
caption:
A 12-year-old Cinebench world record has finally fallen.

The unlikely hero? An ancient Intel Core i5 4670K CPU.

Overclocking expert Luumi has achieved a remarkable feat, breaking a 12-year-old Cinebench R11.5 world record for the Intel Core i5 4670K. The record-breaking score of 10.8 cb was achieved using the Haswell-era quad-core CPU, pushed to an astonishing 6,301 MHz with the aid of liquid nitrogen cooling.

The system featured an ASRock Z97 OC Formula motherboard and 4GB of XPG DDR3 RAM, powered by a Corsair AXi 1600 PSU. This achievement highlights that cutting-edge hardware isn't always necessary to set new performance benchmarks in the overclocking community.

This record is specific to the Core i5 4670K processor category. Despite its age, the 22nm Haswell chip, originally released with a base clock of 3.4 GHz, was pushed to its absolute limits.

The use of older hardware for such achievements is a breath of fresh air for many in the overclocking scene, with community members noting the rarity of seeing results that don't involve the latest X3D CPUs or high-end GPUs.

Luumi utilized Windows 7 64-bit Pro for the benchmark, a common practice for ensuring compatibility and stability with older hardware during extreme overclocking attempts.

headline_marked: Typo-squatting attacks [[still viable]] using Unicode characters in domain names
headline: Typo-squatting attacks still viable using Unicode characters in domain names
summary: Even advanced browsers like Chromium struggle to detect malicious domains that use lookalike characters from different alphabets, posing a persistent threat.
details: The ability to use Unicode characters in domain names, while a boon for internationalization, has opened the door for sophisticated typo-squatting attacks. Attackers register domain names that appear identical to legitimate ones but contain subtle character substitutions, aiming to trick unsuspecting users.

Researchers have demonstrated how specific Cyrillic characters can be used to create domains that evade detection by even the most advanced browser safeguards. For instance, the domain 'аррӏө.com' uses characters that closely resemble Latin letters, making it difficult for users and automated systems to distinguish from 'apple.com'.

While browsers like Chromium have implemented robust rulesets to combat these threats, including lists of known lookalike characters and per-alphabet verifications, edge cases persist. The ever-expanding Unicode character set, with nearly 173,000 entries, makes it a constant challenge to maintain comprehensive detection.

Chromium is considered the best browser in detecting such attacks, reportedly catching over 64% of attempts in a 2020 study. However, this still leaves a significant percentage of potential threats undetected, highlighting the ongoing need for vigilance.

To mitigate the risk, experts recommend that companies proactively register potential lookalike domains. Furthermore, encouraging the use of passkeys can significantly enhance security, as passkeys are tied to specific domains and cannot be used on fraudulent sites.
